grounding_report.claim: Linear regression predicts a continuous number.
Logistic regression predicts a discrete category.
Linear regression and logistic regression are the simplest, most interpretable models for these tasks.
They are the foundation of supervised learning.
Understanding them is essential before moving to neural networks or tree-based models.
They are fast to train, easy to debug, and often serve as a baseline that more complex models must beat.
They also introduce core concepts like loss functions, gradient descent, and regularization that appear everywhere in ML.
Linear regression models the relationship between input features X and a continuous target y as a linear combination: y_pred = w0 + w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + wn*xn.
The weights w are learned by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) loss: L = (1/N) * sum((y_i - y_pred_i)^2).
The optimal weights can be found analytically using the normal equation: w = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y.
But for large datasets, gradient descent is used: w = w - lr * (2/N) * X^T (Xw - y).
Logistic regression is for binary classification.
It applies the sigmoid function to the linear combination: p = 1 / (1 + exp(-(w0 + w1*x1 + ...))).
The output p is the probability of the positive class.
The loss function is binary cross-entropy: L = -(1/N) * sum(y_i * log(p_i) + (1-y_i) * log(1-p_i)).
There is no closed-form solution, so gradient descent is used: w = w - lr * (1/N) * X^T (p - y).
Both models assume linearity.
If the true relationship is nonlinear, they underfit.
They also assume features are independent.
Multicollinearity (correlated features) inflates variance of the weights, making predictions unstable.
Regularization (L1 or L2) can help.
L2 (Ridge) adds a penalty on the sum of squared weights: L_reg = L + lambda * sum(w_j^2).
L1 (Lasso) adds a penalty on absolute values: L_reg = L + lambda * sum(|w_j|).
L1 can drive some weights to zero, performing feature selection.
A common failure mode is using logistic regression on imbalanced datasets.
The model will predict the majority class most of the time.
Techniques like class weighting or oversampling the minority class are needed.
Another failure mode is outliers in linear regression.
A single extreme point can pull the regression line significantly.
Robust regression or outlier removal is required.
Linear regression predicts continuous values by fitting a line (or hyperplane) that minimizes squared error.
Logistic regression predicts probabilities for binary classification using the sigmoid function and cross-entropy loss.
Both models assume linearity and independence of features; violations cause underfitting or unstable weights.
Regularization (L1/L2) prevents overfitting and can perform feature selection.
Gradient descent is the standard optimization method when closed-form solutions are impractical.

grounding_report.claim: Ridge, Lasso, and ElasticNet are regularization techniques that shrink coefficients toward zero, trading a small increase in bias for a large reduction in variance.
Ridge adds an L2 penalty (sum of squared coefficients) to the loss function.
Lasso adds an L1 penalty (sum of absolute coefficients).
ElasticNet combines both penalties, handling correlated features better than Lasso alone.
Ridge never sets coefficients to zero, so all features remain in the model.
Lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero, making it useful for feature selection.
When features are highly correlated, Lasso tends to pick one arbitrarily and ignore the others.
ElasticNet combines both: minimize RSS + alpha * (rho * sum(|w_j|) + (1 - rho) * sum(w_j^2)).
When rho=1, it's Lasso; when rho=0, it's Ridge.
Standardizing features is critical because penalties are scale-sensitive.
ElasticNet requires tuning two hyperparameters, which increases computational cost.
Ridge is safer when you expect all features to be relevant.
Lasso is better when you suspect many features are irrelevant.
ElasticNet is a good default when you don't know the correlation structure.
Cross-validation is used to select alpha (and rho for ElasticNet).
Ridge has a closed form: w_ridge = (X^T X + alpha * I)^{-1} X^T y.
Lasso penalty is not differentiable at zero, so the solution requires coordinate descent or subgradient methods.
If alpha is too large, coefficients become too small and the model underfits.
If alpha is too small, regularization has no effect.
Lasso can be unstable with high multicollinearity.
Ridge shrinks all coefficients but keeps every feature in the model.
Lasso can zero out coefficients, performing automatic feature selection.
Always standardize features before applying these regularizers because penalties are scale-sensitive.
Cross-validation is essential to tune the regularization strength alpha (and l1_ratio for ElasticNet) to avoid underfitting or overfitting.

grounding_report.claim: Support Vector Machines (SVMs) find the hyperplane that maximizes the margin between the nearest points of each class, called support vectors.
The maximum margin principle makes SVMs robust to small perturbations and often yields better generalization on unseen data.
SVMs handle non-linear boundaries through the kernel trick, mapping data into higher dimensions without explicit computation.
SVMs are widely used in text classification, image recognition, and bioinformatics where clear separation and robustness are critical.
For a linearly separable dataset, the hyperplane is defined as w·x + b = 0, where w is the weight vector and b is the bias.
The margin is 2/||w||, so maximizing it is equivalent to minimizing ||w|| subject to the constraint that all points are correctly classified: y_i (w·x_i + b) >= 1 for all i.
This is a convex optimization problem solved via Lagrange multipliers, leading to the dual formulation where only support vectors contribute to the solution.
Soft-margin SVMs introduce slack variables ξ_i to allow misclassifications, with a penalty parameter C controlling the trade-off between margin width and training error.
The objective becomes: minimize (1/2)||w||^2 + C Σ ξ_i, subject to y_i (w·x_i + b) >= 1 - ξ_i, ξ_i >= 0.
A small C gives a wider margin but more misclassifications; a large C penalizes errors heavily, potentially overfitting.
For non-linear boundaries, the kernel trick replaces dot products w·x with a kernel function K(x_i, x_j) that implicitly maps data into a higher-dimensional space.
Common kernels include the polynomial kernel K(x_i, x_j) = (x_i·x_j + r)^d and the radial basis function (RBF) kernel K(x_i, x_j) = exp(-γ ||x_i - x_j||^2).
The RBF kernel is a default choice because it can approximate any continuous function given enough data, but it introduces the hyperparameter γ, which controls the influence of each training example.
A large γ can cause overfitting by making the decision boundary too wiggly.
SVMs are sensitive to feature scaling — all features should be normalized to similar ranges, typically via StandardScaler.
SVMs scale poorly with large datasets (O(n^2) to O(n^3) in training time), making them unsuitable for millions of samples without approximations.
The choice of kernel and hyperparameters (C, γ) requires cross-validation; grid search is common but expensive.
SVMs do not naturally output probabilistic predictions; Platt scaling can be used but adds complexity.
SVMs maximize the margin between classes, leading to better generalization than methods that only minimize training error.
The kernel trick allows SVMs to handle non-linear decision boundaries without explicit feature engineering.
Soft-margin SVMs use a penalty parameter C to control the trade-off between margin width and misclassification tolerance.
SVMs require careful feature scaling and hyperparameter tuning (C, gamma) to avoid poor performance or overfitting.
SVMs are not suitable for very large datasets due to O(n^2) to O(n^3) training complexity.
